q.intro.text: Two hundred eighth graders answered two questions: do you have a curfew, and do you do chores? The table shows their answers. Of the students with a curfew, what percent do chores? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one. The table moves first, then the maths on the board.

e.step0.text: Each student sits in exactly one cell. Add across: one hundred twenty have a curfew, eighty don't. Add down: one hundred sixteen do chores, eighty-four don't. Both ways give all two hundred.

e.step1.text: Of the students with a curfew. That names the whole: the curfew row, one hundred twenty students. The part is where that row meets chores: eighty-four.

e.step2.text: Part over whole: eighty-four divided by one hundred twenty is zero point seven, or seventy percent. The row becomes one bar: all of the curfew students, split seventy percent chores, thirty percent no chores.

e.step3.text: The other row as its own bar: thirty-two of the eighty without a curfew do chores. That's forty percent. Seventy percent against forty percent: the bars split in different places, thirty percentage points apart. Curfew and chores are associated.

e.why.text: Quick check: why is the whole one hundred twenty, and not two hundred?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. Of the students with a curfew narrows it to that row, so those one hundred twenty are the whole.

e.why.all.text: Eighty-four out of two hundred is forty-two percent: the share of all students who have a curfew and do chores. That answers a different question.

e.why.row.text: Not always. Of the students who do chores would make the chores column, one hundred sixteen, the whole.

t.intro.text: Now two hundred fifty students: do you ride the bus, and do you eat school breakfast? Of the breakfast eaters, what percent ride the bus? The first step is done for you.

t.given.text: The totals are in: one hundred twenty ride the bus, one hundred thirty don't. Ninety eat school breakfast, one hundred sixty don't.

t.whole.text: Name the whole: who is the hundred percent here?

t.whole.ok.text: Yes. Of the breakfast eaters makes the breakfast column the whole: ninety students.

t.whole.row.text: That is the bus row. The question says of the breakfast eaters: they are the whole.

t.whole.all.text: All two hundred fifty would be the whole for of all students. Here the question names one group.

t.pct.text: The part is seventy-two: breakfast eaters who ride the bus. What percent of the breakfast eaters is that?

t.pct.ok.text: Right. Seventy-two divided by ninety is zero point eight, or eighty percent. The column drops into one bar.

t.pct.row.text: Sixty percent is seventy-two out of the one hundred twenty bus riders. The whole is the ninety breakfast eaters.

t.pct.all.text: That is seventy-two out of all two hundred fifty. The whole is only the ninety breakfast eaters.

t.pct.count.text: Seventy-two is the count. As a percent of the ninety breakfast eaters, divide.

t.pct.miss.text: Divide the part by the whole: seventy-two divided by ninety.

t.assoc.text: The other column: forty-eight of the one hundred sixty who skip breakfast ride the bus. That's thirty percent. Is there an association?

t.assoc.ok.text: Yes. Eighty percent against thirty percent. The bars split in very different places.

t.assoc.size.text: Group sizes don't decide it. Compare the shares: eighty percent of one group, thirty percent of the other.

t.assoc.cause.text: The data show a link, not a cause. Maybe bus riders just get to school in time for breakfast.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked seventy percent, and you were right. Now you can say why: the curfew row is the whole.

q.cb.all.text: At the start you picked forty-two percent. That divides by all two hundred: it answers of all students, not of the curfew students.

q.cb.col.text: At the start you picked about seventy-two percent. That divides by the chores column, one hundred sixteen: it answers of the students who do chores.

q.cb.none.text: Name the whole first: the group after the words of the. Then divide the part by it.

p.intro.text: A survey of three hundred students: music lessons and sports. Jordan says: one hundred twenty is the biggest number in the table, so music students are more likely to play a sport. Is Jordan right?

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. The music row is big: one hundred eighty of the three hundred. A big group makes a big cell, whatever the share.

p.c2.text: Right. Out of the one hundred eighty music students, one hundred twenty play a sport: about sixty-six point seven percent.

p.c3.text: Right. Out of the one hundred twenty others, eighty play a sport: about sixty-six point seven percent too. The bars split at the same place.

p.no.cell.text: That is Jordan's reason itself. A big cell can just mean a big group.

p.no.all.text: One hundred twenty out of three hundred is the share of everybody. For music students, the whole is the one hundred eighty of them.

p.no.cause.text: A survey can't show a cause, and here there isn't even an association to explain.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That's a proof: three claims, each with its reason. Same split in both groups: no association, even though one hundred twenty is the biggest cell.
